title: Episode 32: GitHub Mobile
description: VoiceOver and TalkBack guide for iOS and Android GitHub apps.
concepts: What GitHub Mobile offers: issues, PRs, notifications, code browsing
VoiceOver navigation on iOS: swipe gestures, rotor usage
TalkBack navigation on Android: swipe gestures, explore by touch
Viewing and triaging notifications on mobile
Reviewing pull request diffs on a small screen
Current accessibility limitations of GitHub Mobile
When mobile is useful versus when to use the desktop or web
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're focusing on GitHub Mobile: what it is, how to get around it, and how to use it accessibly on iOS and Android.

[JAMIE]
And this feels especially useful for people who don't always want to open a laptop just to check a review request or respond to an issue.

[ALEX]
Exactly. GitHub Mobile is best understood as a companion workflow. It brings issues, pull requests, notifications, and code review to iPhone, iPad, and Android devices. For many learners, especially blind and low-vision contributors, it can be a very practical way to stay engaged when away from the desktop.

[JAMIE]
So this isn't, "replace your whole Git workflow with a phone."

[ALEX]
Right. It is not your full desktop environment. You are not doing heavy branch management, conflict resolution, or large-scale coding comfortably in the app. But for triage, quick reviews, comments, issue management, and keeping up with team activity, it can be excellent.

[JAMIE]
Before we go farther, can we do a fast mental map of the app for different kinds of users?

[ALEX]
Yes. For screen reader users, GitHub Mobile supports VoiceOver on iOS and TalkBack on Android natively. A common pattern is swipe right to move to the next element, swipe left to move back, and double tap to activate. The app is organized around five bottom tabs, and that tab bar is one of the main navigation landmarks.

For low-vision users, the app respects system text sizing, supports dark mode, and generally presents information in simpler mobile layouts. One especially important example is pull request diffs: on mobile they appear in a simplified single-column form rather than the more visually dense desktop diff table.

For sighted users, the same structure applies: bottom tabs, notification badges, quick actions by swiping notifications, and a mobile-optimized PR diff view.

[JAMIE]
So even though our audience here is blind and low vision, it's helpful to know the visual model too, because people collaborate across different access preferences.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
A quick administrative note. This appendix is a reference companion to the material on working with issues, and it's also closely connected to notifications workflows. And if you ever need the current source of truth, use GitHub Docs and the GitHub changelog, because mobile apps change over time.

[JAMIE]
That's a really important reminder. A button name or gesture support detail may shift as the app evolves.

[ALEX]
Yes. So learn the concepts, then verify the latest details in the official documentation.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's start with setup. Installing GitHub Mobile is straightforward. On iOS, you download GitHub from the App Store. On Android, you download it from Google Play.

[JAMIE]
Then sign in with your GitHub account.

[ALEX]
Right. And when the app asks whether to enable notifications, say yes if you want mobile to be genuinely useful. Notifications are central to the whole experience. They let you know about review requests, mentions, issue updates, and other activity without repeatedly checking the website.

[JAMIE]
So if someone installs the app but disables notifications, they may miss the app's biggest advantage.

[ALEX]
That's exactly it.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Once you're in, the app is organized around five tabs at the bottom of the screen.

[JAMIE]
Let's name them slowly, because this is the core map.

[ALEX]
Home, Notifications, Explore, Pull Requests, and Profile.

Home is your personalized activity feed across repositories. Notifications is where mentions, review requests, and issue updates appear. Explore helps you discover repositories and trending projects. Pull Requests collects PRs assigned to you, created by you, or waiting for your review. And Profile contains your own profile information, repositories, stars, and settings.

[JAMIE]
For a screen reader user, that tab bar becomes a repeated anchor point.

[ALEX]
Yes. On iOS with VoiceOver, you might swipe across the bottom to move between tabs, then double tap to activate. Sighted users may single tap directly. The important idea is that these five tabs define the app's main structure.

[JAMIE]
And if someone gets lost, returning to the tab bar can re-orient them.

[ALEX]
Exactly right.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let's turn to iOS and VoiceOver.

[JAMIE]
Starting with the basics: how do you turn VoiceOver on?

[ALEX]
Two common ways. You can triple-click the side button on newer iPhones, or the Home button on older devices, if that accessibility shortcut is configured. Or you can go through Settings, then Accessibility, then VoiceOver, and toggle it on.

[JAMIE]
Once VoiceOver is running, what gestures matter most inside GitHub Mobile?

[ALEX]
The essential set is: swipe right for next element, swipe left for previous element, double tap to activate the focused item, two-finger swipe up to read from the top, two-finger tap to pause or resume speech, three-finger swipe left or right to move between screens, and the two-finger scrub, that Z-shaped gesture, to go back.

[JAMIE]
That last one is especially nice on iOS because it gives you a quick escape route.

[ALEX]
Yes. If you've gone into a notification or opened a pull request and want to return, scrub can be very efficient.

[JAMIE]
What about the rotor? Because that's one of the most powerful VoiceOver tools, and many learners underuse it.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. In GitHub Mobile, the rotor can make navigation much faster. You open it by rotating two fingers on the screen as though turning a dial. Useful rotor settings here include Headings, Links, Form Controls, and Actions.

Headings helps you jump between sections in an issue or pull request description. Links helps you move through linked issues, commits, or external URLs. Form Controls can take you directly to interactive fields, such as a comment box. And Actions can expose operations related to the focused element, such as assign, label, or close, when those actions are available.

[JAMIE]
So if a learner is swiping endlessly through a long PR description, the advice is: stop, use the rotor, switch to Headings.

[ALEX]
Exactly. That's one of the highest-value accessibility habits in the app.

[JAMIE]
And if they want to comment?

[ALEX]
A typical VoiceOver workflow is: navigate to the comment field, either by swiping or by using the rotor set to Form Controls. Double tap to activate the field and bring up the keyboard. Type the comment, with VoiceOver announcing characters as you enter them. Then swipe until you reach the Comment button and double tap to submit.

[JAMIE]
That sounds simple, but it's worth stating because forms on mobile can feel disorienting.

[ALEX]
Yes, especially when focus shifts unexpectedly or the keyboard changes the layout. A deliberate pattern helps.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let's look at Android with TalkBack.

[JAMIE]
How do you enable it?

[ALEX]
You can go to Settings, then Accessibility, then TalkBack, and toggle it on. Many Android devices also support a shortcut by holding both volume keys for three seconds, if that shortcut has been enabled.

[JAMIE]
And the core gestures?

[ALEX]
Much like VoiceOver in spirit, though not identical in detail. Swipe right for the next element, swipe left for the previous one, double tap to activate. Swipe up then down to scroll down. Swipe down then up to scroll up. Swipe right then left to go back. And two-finger swipe down to read from the top.

[JAMIE]
One thing that helps learners is remembering that screen readers often share a navigation philosophy even when the exact gestures differ.

[ALEX]
Well said. Learn the pattern: move, activate, read continuously, go back, adjust granularity.

[JAMIE]
That brings us to the TalkBack menu.

[ALEX]
Yes. You can open the TalkBack menu with a three-finger tap, or on some setups by swiping down then right. In that menu, you can do things like change reading granularity to character, word, line, or paragraph; access reading controls; and copy text.

[JAMIE]
Why does granularity matter in GitHub Mobile?

[ALEX]
Because technical text can be dense. If you're reviewing a pull request, reading an issue description, or trying to inspect a changed line, the ability to move by character or word can be essential. It gives you finer control than simply swiping element by element.

[JAMIE]
And writing a comment with TalkBack?

[ALEX]
The common pattern is: locate the comment field, which TalkBack may announce as something like "Edit text, double tap to edit." Double tap to enter the field. Type using the on-screen keyboard or dictation. Then locate the Comment button and double tap to submit.

[JAMIE]
So the iOS and Android workflows are parallel, even though the screen reader mechanics differ.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now to one of the strongest parts of GitHub Mobile: notifications.

[JAMIE]
This is where mobile can actually be better than the website for some accessibility users, right?

[ALEX]
Very often, yes. The Notifications tab presents activity in a clean, linear list. For assistive technology users, especially screen reader users, that can be much easier to navigate than a more crowded web page.

[JAMIE]
Let's paint the picture.

[ALEX]
Each notification appears as an item in a chronological list. Unread items typically have an unread indicator. For sighted users, that may be a blue dot on the left. The row also includes useful context like repository name, notification type, and title. For screen reader users, swiping through the list one item at a time can make triage very manageable.

[JAMIE]
And there are quick actions too.

[ALEX]
Yes. Swipe left on a notification to reveal actions such as Mark as read, Archive, and Unsubscribe. In some contexts, swiping right can mark a notification as done. Tapping the notification opens the underlying issue or pull request.

[JAMIE]
How does this translate for VoiceOver users, since swipe gestures can mean navigation rather than app-specific actions?

[ALEX]
Great question. On iOS, custom actions may be available through the VoiceOver Actions rotor item on each notification. So instead of relying purely on sighted-style swipe gestures, a VoiceOver user can focus the notification, switch the rotor to Actions, and then perform the available action.

[JAMIE]
That's a very helpful clarification.

[ALEX]
Filtering is another important feature. At the top right of the Notifications tab, there is a filter control, often represented visually by a funnel icon. You can filter by type, such as issues, pull requests, or releases; by repository; and by reason, such as being mentioned, assigned, or asked to review.

[JAMIE]
And with a screen reader?

[ALEX]
Those filters should appear as accessible form elements. Open the filter panel, navigate through the available controls, and toggle the criteria you want. This lets you narrow a busy inbox to the most relevant activity.

[JAMIE]
So if someone says, "My notifications are overwhelming," the answer is not just archive more. It's also filter intelligently.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Filter by reason, filter by repository, and use quick actions aggressively.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's move into pull requests. Mobile is well suited to quick PR review: checking status, reading the description, scanning changed files, and leaving an approval or short comment.

[JAMIE]
But maybe not a forty-file architectural review on a phone.

[ALEX]
Correct. Use the right tool for the task.

When you open a pull request in GitHub Mobile, you'll generally encounter a few main sections: the Description, the Commits list, Files changed, and Checks for CI or other status information.

[JAMIE]
And these are often announced as headings.

[ALEX]
Yes. That's important. VoiceOver users can use the rotor set to Headings to jump among those sections. TalkBack users can use heading navigation or reading granularity methods available on their device. That means you don't have to swipe through every single element in sequence.

[JAMIE]
Let's walk through leaving a review.

[ALEX]
A typical flow is: find the Review changes button, activate it, choose whether you want to Approve, Request changes, or Comment, optionally add text in the review comment field, and then activate Submit review.

[JAMIE]
So the review is not just a comment; it's a structured decision.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Approve means the changes look good. Request changes signals that the author should revise something before merge. Comment lets you leave feedback without explicitly approving or blocking.

[JAMIE]
And viewing diffs on mobile has a distinct accessibility advantage.

[ALEX]
It often does. In the Files Changed area, GitHub Mobile uses a simplified diff. Additions and removals are shown as text rather than forcing you through a two-column desktop-style table. Changed lines may be announced in a direct way, such as "Added" followed by content, or "Removed" followed by content.

[JAMIE]
That can be easier to understand with a screen reader than a dense side-by-side layout.

[ALEX]
Yes. On a small screen, the simpler structure can actually improve access.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let's talk about issues.

[JAMIE]
This is one of the most practical mobile tasks: filing something when you notice it, instead of telling yourself you'll remember later.

[ALEX]
Exactly. To file an issue, you generally navigate to the repository, choose Issues, then find the plus button or New Issue. Enter the title and body. Optionally set labels, assignees, and a milestone if those are part of the workflow. Then submit the issue.

[JAMIE]
Even if the source text was truncated there, the workflow is clear: repository, issues, new issue, fill in fields, optionally set metadata, submit.

[ALEX]
Right. And those optional fields matter in team workflows. Labels classify the issue, assignees indicate responsibility, and milestones connect the issue to a broader goal or release.

[JAMIE]
What about finding issues that matter to you?

[ALEX]
In mobile, you can use your notifications, repository issue lists, and your personal areas in the app to return to issues you've opened, been assigned, or been mentioned in. The core idea is to combine repository navigation with notification-driven access, rather than hunting manually every time.

[JAMIE]
So for many learners, notifications become the front door to issue work too.

[ALEX]
Very much so.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
At this point it's worth stepping back and asking: what does mobile do well, and what should remain a desktop task?

[JAMIE]
Let's make that explicit.

[ALEX]
GitHub Mobile does well at staying current. Notifications, quick triage, lightweight issue filing, short comments, straightforward PR reviews, and checking checks or CI status are all good mobile tasks. The interface is linear, compact, and often easier for assistive technology users than a more cluttered desktop page.

[JAMIE]
And desktop still wins for deep work.

[ALEX]
Yes. If you need to read a very large pull request, compare lots of files, manage complicated issue templates, perform substantial code editing, resolve merge conflicts, or do anything that depends on a full Git client and development environment, desktop is the better choice.

[JAMIE]
So mobile is not lesser. It's specialized.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Think of it as the right tool for quick response and continuous awareness.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's finish with common issues and workarounds, because these practical frustrations matter.

[JAMIE]
First: VoiceOver skips some pull request descriptions.

[ALEX]
A good workaround is to switch the rotor to Headings or Links and navigate by structure instead of plain sequential swiping. If the description contains complex formatting, try moving by headings, then by links, and explore the content in smaller pieces. If necessary, reopen the item or use another navigation mode rather than assuming the content is absent.

[JAMIE]
Second: TalkBack does not announce the new notifications badge.

[ALEX]
In that case, don't rely only on the badge. Open the Notifications tab directly and review the list. Mobile badges can be inconsistent across apps and devices, so the reliable method is to check the tab itself.

[JAMIE]
Third: the keyboard covers the comment field.

[ALEX]
This is a common mobile problem. After activating the comment field, you may need to scroll slightly, dismiss and reopen the keyboard, rotate the device if your setup allows, or move focus carefully until the submit control comes back into view. On either platform, patience and incremental navigation help.

[JAMIE]
Fourth: after writing a review, you can't find the Submit button.

[ALEX]
This often means focus is still trapped near the keyboard or text field. Try navigating past the editing area deliberately. On iOS, rotor settings like Form Controls can help jump among interactive elements. On Android, move through controls methodically or adjust granularity if needed. If the button still doesn't appear, dismiss the keyboard and continue exploring the screen.

[JAMIE]
And fifth: the app crashes or freezes.

[ALEX]
The practical steps are the usual ones: force close and reopen the app, make sure it's updated, and if the problem persists, sign out and sign back in through Profile and Settings. If you still cannot complete the task, switch to the web or desktop workflow so your work is not blocked.

[JAMIE]
That's an important accessibility principle in itself: have a fallback path.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. Accessibility isn't only about one perfect interface. It's also about knowing alternate routes when a tool becomes unreliable.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Can we close with a compact recap?

[ALEX]
Certainly. GitHub Mobile gives you five main tabs for navigation: Home, Notifications, Explore, Pull Requests, and Profile. On iOS, VoiceOver users rely on familiar gestures and especially the rotor, with Headings, Form Controls, Links, and Actions being especially valuable. On Android, TalkBack users use core swipe and activation gestures, plus the TalkBack menu for reading granularity and controls.

Notifications are one of the strongest mobile features, because they provide a clean linear inbox with filtering and quick actions. Pull request review works well for lightweight review, comments, and approvals, with a simplified diff view that can be more accessible than desktop on a small screen. Issues can be filed and managed on mobile, especially for quick capture and response. And throughout all of this, mobile is best seen as a companion to desktop rather than a full replacement.

[JAMIE]
And if learners want the latest details, they should check GitHub Docs, the GitHub Mobile docs specifically, and the GitHub changelog.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Official references matter, because apps evolve.

[JAMIE]
That was a practical one.

[ALEX]
It was. And for many contributors, mastering mobile means staying connected to open source and team workflows in the moments between full desktop sessions.

[PAUSE]

# Appendix V: GitHub Mobile
>
> **Listen to Episode 32:** [GitHub Mobile](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Reference companion to:** [Chapter 05: Working with Issues](05-working-with-issues.md) | Also relevant: [Chapter 10](10-notifications-and-day-1-close.md)
>
> **Authoritative source:** [GitHub Docs: GitHub Mobile](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/github-mobile)

## Accessibility Guide for iOS and Android

> GitHub Mobile brings issues, pull requests, notifications, and code review to your iPhone, iPad, or Android device. This appendix covers setup, VoiceOver and TalkBack usage, and the tasks best suited to mobile.

### Learning Cards: GitHub Mobile Overview

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- GitHub Mobile supports VoiceOver (iOS) and TalkBack (Android) natively -- swipe right to move through elements, double-tap to activate
- The app uses five bottom tabs (Home, Notifications, Explore, Pull Requests, Profile) -- swipe left or right along the bottom tab bar to switch between them
- Use the VoiceOver Rotor (two-finger twist) set to Headings to jump between sections within an issue or PR description

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- GitHub Mobile supports dynamic text sizing on both iOS and Android -- increase your system font size and the app respects it
- Dark mode is available in the app settings and follows your system preference -- use it to reduce glare on OLED screens
- The simplified diff view in Files Changed shows additions and removals as text only, without the two-column table layout used on desktop

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The five-tab navigation bar at the bottom of the screen (Home, Notifications, Explore, Pull Requests, Profile) is your primary way around the app
- Notification badges appear as red dots on the Notifications tab -- swipe left on individual notifications for quick actions (read, archive, unsubscribe)
- Pull request diffs use a simplified single-column view optimized for small screens -- additions appear in green, removals in red

</details>

## Table of Contents

1. [Installing GitHub Mobile](#1-installing-github-mobile)
2. [Getting Around the App](#2-getting-around-the-app)
3. [VoiceOver on iOS](#3-voiceover-on-ios)
4. [TalkBack on Android](#4-talkback-on-android)
5. [Working with Notifications](#5-working-with-notifications)
6. [Reviewing Pull Requests](#6-reviewing-pull-requests)
7. [Working with Issues](#7-working-with-issues)
8. [What Mobile Does Well vs. Desktop](#8-what-mobile-does-well-vs-desktop)
9. [Common Issues and Workarounds](#9-common-issues-and-workarounds)

## 1. Installing GitHub Mobile

| Platform | Download |
| ----------  | ----------  |
| iOS (iPhone / iPad) | [App Store - GitHub](https://apps.apple.com/app/github/id1477376905) |
| Android | [Google Play - GitHub](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.github.android) |

After installing, sign in with your GitHub account. Enable notifications when prompted - these are essential for staying on top of PR reviews and issue activity without constantly checking the web.

## 2. Getting Around the App

GitHub Mobile is organized into five main tabs at the bottom of the screen:

| Tab | Contents |
| -----  | ----------  |
| Home | Personalized feed of activity across your repositories |
| Notifications | All @mentions, review requests, issue updates |
| Explore | Discover repositories and trending projects |
| Pull Requests | PRs assigned to you, created by you, or awaiting your review |
| Profile | Your profile, repositories, stars, and settings |

Navigate between tabs with a single tap (or swipe on iOS with VoiceOver active).

## 3. VoiceOver on iOS

### Enabling VoiceOver

- **Triple-click the side button** (iPhone X and later) or triple-click the Home button to toggle VoiceOver
- Or: Settings → Accessibility → VoiceOver → toggle on

### Basic Gestures in GitHub Mobile

| Gesture | Action |
| ---------  | --------  |
| Swipe right | Move to the next element |
| Swipe left | Move to the previous element |
| Double tap | Activate the focused element |
| Two-finger swipe up | Read from the top |
| Two-finger tap | Pause/resume speech |
| Three-finger swipe left/right | Move between screens |
| Scrub (two-finger Z motion) | Go back |

### Rotor in GitHub Mobile

Open the Rotor by rotating two fingers on the screen as if turning a dial. Useful rotor settings for GitHub Mobile:

- **Headings** - jump between section headings on an issue or PR description
- **Links** - navigate to linked issues, commits, or external URLs
- **Form Controls** - jump to input fields when writing a comment
- **Actions** - available actions for the focused element (assign, label, close)

### Writing Comments with VoiceOver

1. Navigate to the comment field (swipe to it or use Rotor → Form Controls)
2. Double tap to activate and open the keyboard
3. Type your comment; VoiceOver announces each character
4. When done, swipe to the **Comment** button and double tap to submit

## 4. TalkBack on Android

### Enabling TalkBack

- Settings → Accessibility → TalkBack → toggle on
- Or: hold both volume keys for three seconds (if the shortcut is enabled)

### Basic Gestures in GitHub Mobile

| Gesture | Action |
| ---------  | --------  |
| Swipe right | Move to next element |
| Swipe left | Move to previous element |
| Double tap | Activate the focused element |
| Swipe up then down | Scroll down |
| Swipe down then up | Scroll up |
| Swipe right then left | Go back |
| Two-finger swipe down | Read from top |

### TalkBack Menu

Tap with three fingers (or swipe down then right) to open the TalkBack menu. From here you can:

- Change the reading granularity (character, word, line, paragraph)
- Activate reading controls
- Copy text

### Writing Comments with TalkBack

1. Locate the comment field - TalkBack announces "Edit text, double tap to edit"
2. Double tap to enter the field
3. Use the on-screen keyboard or dictation to type
4. Locate the **Comment** button and double tap to submit

## 5. Working with Notifications

GitHub Mobile's Notifications tab is one of its strongest features for AT users - it surfaces all activity in a clean, linear list that is much easier to navigate than the GitHub web notifications page.

### Learning Cards: Mobile Notifications

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- The Notifications tab presents a linear list that is more accessible than the web version -- swipe right through items one by one to hear each notification's context
- Filter controls are accessible form elements at the top -- navigate to the filter icon, activate it, then swipe through filter options (Type, Repository, Reason)
- Swipe actions (left to archive, right to mark done) work with VoiceOver custom actions -- use the VoiceOver Actions rotor item on each notification

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Notifications are displayed as a vertical list with the repository name, notification type, and title on each row -- text is sized according to your system accessibility settings
- The filter panel overlays on top of the list -- look for the funnel icon in the top-right corner of the Notifications tab
- Unread notifications appear with a blue dot indicator on the left edge of each row

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The Notifications tab shows all activity in a chronological list -- unread items have a blue dot on the left
- Swipe left on any notification to reveal quick-action buttons: Mark as Read, Archive, and Unsubscribe
- Use the filter icon (top right) to narrow by notification type, repository, or reason (mentioned, review requested, assigned)

</details>

### Inbox Management

- **Swipe left** on a notification to reveal quick actions: Mark as read, Archive, Unsubscribe
- **Swipe right** to mark as done
- Tap a notification to open the full issue or PR

### Filtering Notifications

Use the filter icon at the top right to filter by:

- Type (Issues, PRs, Releases, etc.)
- Repository
- Reason (you were @mentioned, a review was requested, etc.)

With VoiceOver or TalkBack, the filter controls are accessible form elements. Open the filter panel, navigate to each option, and activate to toggle it.

## 6. Reviewing Pull Requests

Mobile is well suited for quick PR reviews - approving straightforward changes, leaving a comment, or checking CI status while away from your desk.

### Navigating a PR

When you open a pull request, the screen is divided into sections:

- **Description** - the PR body with any images or checklists
- **Commits** - individual commits in this PR
- **Files changed** - a simplified diff view
- **Checks** - CI/CD status

VoiceOver and TalkBack announce these as headings. Use heading navigation (Rotor on iOS, swipe granularity on Android) to jump between sections.

### Leaving a Review

1. Scroll to or navigate to the **Review changes** button
2. Double tap to open the review panel
3. Choose Approve, Request changes, or Comment
4. Add an optional comment in the text field
5. Activate **Submit review**

### Viewing Diffs

The Files Changed tab shows a simplified diff - additions and removals are text-only (no table layout). Each changed line is announced as "Added: [content]" or "Removed: [content]", which is generally more accessible than the web diff table on small screens.

## 7. Working with Issues

### Filing an Issue

1. Navigate to the repository
2. Tap **Issues** → the **+** button or **New Issue**
3. Fill in the title and body
4. Optionally assign labels, assignees, and milestone - each is a tappable field
5. Tap **Submit**

### Finding Your Issues

- Pull Requests tab → **Created by you** or **Assigned to you** filters
- For issues: Home feed shows recent activity; or navigate to a specific repository → Issues → filter by Assignee, Label, or Author

## 8. What Mobile Does Well vs. Desktop

| Task | Mobile | Desktop |
| ------  | --------  | ---------  |
| Triage notifications | Excellent - linear list, swipe actions | Good |
| Quick review / approve a PR | Good | Good |
| Writing long PR descriptions | Fair - small keyboard | Better |
| Reviewing large diffs | Fair - simplified view | Better |
| Filing a simple issue | Good | Good |
| Complex issue templates | Fair | Better |
| Managing labels and milestones | Good | Good |
| Reading code | Fair - no syntax highlighting | Better |
| Running Codespace / editing code | Not supported | Supported |

**Best use of GitHub Mobile:** notification triage, quick approvals and comments, catching up on activity between sessions. For writing substantial code, descriptions, or reviewing complex diffs, use the web or VS Code.

## 9. Common Issues and Workarounds

### VoiceOver skips some PR descriptions

Long PR descriptions with images, tables, or embedded videos may not read cleanly. Open the PR in Safari instead - tap the **…** menu → **Open in Browser**.

### TalkBack does not announce new notifications badge

The badge count on the Notifications tab updates live but may not be announced. Navigate directly to the Notifications tab to get the current count read aloud.

### The keyboard covers the comment field

Usual iOS/Android behavior - scroll up slightly after the keyboard appears, or rotate to landscape mode to gain more visible space.

### Can't find the Submit button after writing a review

Scroll down past the text field; buttons are below the keyboard dismiss area. On iOS, tap elsewhere to dismiss the keyboard first, then scroll to Submit.

### GitHub Mobile crashes or freezes

Force close the app and reopen. If the problem persists, sign out and back in via Profile → Settings → Sign out.

---

*Next: [Appendix W: GitHub Pages](appendix-w-github-pages.md)*  
*Back: [Appendix U: Discussions and Gists](appendix-u-discussions-and-gists.md)*  
*Teaching chapter: [Chapter 05: Working with Issues](05-working-with-issues.md)*

currentFacts: The Accessibility Agents collection grows over time. Refer to it as a living catalog rather than asserting a fixed count of agents.
Challenge 15 (Discover Accessibility Agents) is browse-first. Learners are not required to fork the accessibility-agents repository to complete it.
Completing Challenge 15 unlocks Challenge 16 (Capstone Project) plus Bonus Challenges A through E. The bonus challenges are a structured unlock path, not "things to do if you finish early".

Challenge 16 is titled "Capstone Project". It accepts contributions to Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or any other meaningful repository. Review-ready drafts and contribution plans are valid evidence of completion.
The Learning Room repository is where Day 1 contributions happen (issue, branch, commit, pull request, merge). It is provisioned per learner.
Hosts are Alex (warm expert) and Jamie (curious co-host who asks the questions learners hesitate to ask). They are colleagues, not teacher and student.
voiceRules.voiceExemplar:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
